caseStudies.client: Department of Health and Social Care
caseStudies.headline: Compass: a proof-of-concept service for evidence-based medical device procurement
caseStudies.summary: A new service to help NHS clinicians and procurement teams select medical devices based on trusted evidence, peer adoption and patient outcomes.
clientParas: The Department of Health and Social Care wanted to test a new idea: a service, called Compass, that would help NHS clinicians and procurement teams choose medical devices using trusted evidence, peer adoption and patient outcomes, enabling safer, value-based purchasing decisions.
challengeParas: Device procurement decisions are spread across clinicians, procurement teams and suppliers, with evidence scattered across trials, registries and peer experience. The department needed to know what such a service would do, who it was for and whether it was worth building, before committing to development.
objectives: Define the product and its users through a series of stakeholder workshops
Map the end-to-end service as a blueprint, including the evidence sources and the people behind each step
Bring the concept to life with storyboards and early prototypes
Give the department a proof of concept it could test and take to a funding decision
approachParas: We ran a series of workshops with clinical, procurement and policy stakeholders to define what Compass should do and where it would sit in existing processes. From that we created a service blueprint, initial storyboards and prototypes that showed how a clinician or buyer would move from a need to a confident, evidence-backed choice.
The prototypes drew on current AI models to surface and summarise evidence, with a clear human decision at the end of every journey.
resultParas: The department has a defined proof of concept, a service blueprint and tested prototypes to take forward. Engagement ran from September 2025 to March 2026.

caseStudies.headline: Redesigning how court hearings are scheduled and listed
caseStudies.summary: Defining the as-is and to-be processes for scheduling and listing court hearings, grounded in interviews with the people who do it every day.
clientParas: The Ministry of Justice is modernising how hearings are scheduled and listed across the courts. The work needed a clear picture of how listing happens today and a designed future state that the digital team could build towards.
challengeParas: Listing involves judges, listing officers, legal professionals and court staff working with constraints that are rarely written down. The to-be process had to reflect those realities, not an idealised version of them.
objectives: Define the as-is scheduling and listing processes with the stakeholders who run them
Interview end users to establish the real pain points
Create the to-be journey based on the agreed epics and user stories
Design the landing pages for the new service
approachParas: We worked with Ministry of Justice stakeholders to document the as-is and to-be processes for scheduling and listing. We interviewed end users to establish pain points, then designed the to-be journey and the landing pages for the service, working from the epics and user stories agreed with the product team.
resultParas: The programme has an evidenced as-is picture, a to-be journey and designed landing pages for the next phase of delivery. Our engagement ran from May to October 2026.

caseStudies.headline: Programme-level service blueprint for Making Tax Digital
caseStudies.summary: Mapping as-is and to-be customer journeys across the Making Tax Digital programme and bringing them together in a single programme-level blueprint.
clientParas: Making Tax Digital is HMRC’s programme to move tax reporting to digital record keeping and quarterly updates for businesses and landlords. It spans many teams, services and software providers.
challengeParas: Each part of the programme understood its own journey, but there was no single view of how a customer moved through the whole thing, where the pain points were, or where different services overlapped or contradicted each other.
objectives: Map the as-is and to-be customer journeys
Identify pain points and opportunities to optimise processes and interactions
Create a programme-level blueprint across all Making Tax Digital activities
approachParas: We mapped the as-is and to-be customer journeys with the teams involved and identified the pain points that caused customers to stall, call or get it wrong. We then built a programme-level service blueprint that connected every activity across the programme, giving leaders and delivery teams one shared picture.
resultParas: HMRC has a programme-level blueprint and optimised journeys to plan and prioritise against. Engagement ran from January to June 2025.

caseStudies.headline: Researching the future of electric vehicle charging
caseStudies.summary: Testing new product concepts and researching user needs for bp pulse through qualitative and quantitative studies.
clientParas: bp pulse is bp’s electric vehicle charging business, developing new products and services for drivers at home, at work and on the road.
challengeParas: New product areas needed evidence before investment: did drivers understand the concepts, would they use them, and where did the proposed journeys break down?
objectives: Test new product concepts with a broad range of drivers
Research user needs through qualitative and quantitative studies
Run usability sessions on new product development areas
Identify opportunities and service-level blueprints across the EV charging projects
approachParas: We ran usability sessions and concept tests with a broad range of participants, combining qualitative interviews with quantitative studies to size what we found. The research informed service-level blueprints and identified opportunities across a range of EV charging projects.
resultParas: bp pulse product teams had evidence on user needs and concept performance to shape their roadmap. Engagement ran from June to October 2024.

caseStudies.headline: User research for a website redesign
caseStudies.summary: Qualitative and quantitative research to identify demand and validate the user journeys and usability of a new website for the WLGA.
clientParas: The Welsh Local Government Association represents the 22 local authorities in Wales and was redesigning its website to serve members, officers and the public better.
challengeParas: The organisation needed to know what its audiences actually came to the site for, whether the proposed journeys matched that demand, and whether the new design was usable before it launched.
objectives: Identify demand across the WLGA’s audiences
Validate the proposed user journeys
Test the usability of the new design with representative users
approachParas: We ran a programme of qualitative and quantitative research with members, officers and public users to establish demand, then validated the user journeys and tested the usability of the new design, feeding findings back to the design team in each iteration.
resultParas: The redesign launched with journeys and content shaped by evidence from its real audiences. Engagement ran from January to June 2024.

caseStudies.headline: Two years of research into in-store colleague tools
caseStudies.summary: Discovery and proof-of-concept research for mobile devices and interfaces used by store colleagues for security, stock and deliveries.
clientParas: Tesco continually develops the mobile devices and interfaces its store colleagues use to manage security, stock and deliveries. Rolling out a new tool to thousands of stores needs confidence that it works on the shop floor.
challengeParas: Store initiatives ranged from early discovery to proof of concept. Each needed evidence from colleagues working in real conditions, and findings that senior management could act on.
objectives: Run discovery and proof-of-concept research for new mobile devices and interfaces
Use one-to-one research, usability testing, ethnographic observation and surveys
Translate findings into user stories and customer journey maps
Present findings to senior management up to director level
approachParas: Over two years we combined one-to-one research, usability testing and ethnographic research in stores with quantitative survey work. We translated the synthesis into user stories and journey maps for the product teams and presented findings to senior management up to director level.
resultParas: Tesco’s in-store initiatives were shaped by colleague evidence throughout, from discovery to proof of concept. Engagement ran from 2021 to June 2023.

caseStudies.headline: Discovery for a new service for benefit claimants
caseStudies.summary: Designing and testing a new service in discovery, with research participants recruited for accessibility needs, as part of a GDS Beta assessment.
clientParas: The Department for Work and Pensions was exploring a new service for benefit claimants and needed to understand their needs before committing to design.
challengeParas: The service had to work for people with a wide range of accessibility needs and circumstances, and the evidence had to stand up to a GDS assessment.
objectives: Design and test the new service concept in discovery
Create a service blueprint for the end-to-end service
Bring the pain points to life for the client with a visual, multimedia persona journey
Recruit users with accessibility needs to identify their requirements
approachParas: Working in a multidisciplinary team, we created a service blueprint and a visual, multimedia persona journey that brought claimants’ pain points to life for stakeholders. Participants were recruited for accessibility needs so that the service would be human-centred for the people who depend on it most.
resultParas: The work formed part of a GDS Beta assessment and gave the department a human-centred, strategic direction for the service. Engagement ran from July to September 2021.

caseStudies.client: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
caseStudies.headline: Discovery for a new housing options service
caseStudies.summary: A feasibility discovery for a housing management system for citizens who need new housing options, taken through a GDS Alpha assessment.
clientParas: The department wanted to establish the feasibility of a new housing management system for citizens who need new housing options.
challengeParas: The end-to-end process crossed local authorities, landlords and citizens in difficult circumstances. The team needed a blueprint of that process and the evidence to pass an alpha assessment.
objectives: Assess the feasibility of the new service
Design the service blueprint for tracking the end-to-end process
Work in the open with researchers, product managers, interaction and content designers
Get the project through its GDS Alpha assessment
approachParas: We designed the service blueprint for the end-to-end process and worked in an agile, open team with researchers, product managers, interaction designers and content designers to prepare the evidence for assessment.
resultParas: The project passed its GDS Alpha assessment and was scoped for a beta development phase. Engagement ran in June and July 2021.

caseStudies.client: Department of Health and Social Care
caseStudies.headline: Journeys and blueprints for Test and Trace and Community Testing
caseStudies.summary: Mapping ideal customer journeys and service blueprints across the Test and Trace and Community Testing digital programmes.
clientParas: During the pandemic the Test and Trace and Community Testing programmes were developing digital services at speed across many teams and suppliers.
challengeParas: Stakeholders needed visibility of developments across the programme, and a shared picture of the ideal customer journey so that the different services joined up for the public.
objectives: Gain visibility of developments across the Community Testing programme
Map ideal customer journeys and service blueprints for the digital programmes
Complete additional stakeholder research
Help provide a workable strategic solution for delivering testing packs to end consumers
approachParas: We worked with Community Testing stakeholders to map the ideal customer journeys and service blueprints across the programmes, completed further stakeholder research and helped shape a workable strategic solution for getting testing packs to people.
resultParas: The programmes had shared journeys and blueprints to coordinate delivery against. Engagement ran from March to June 2021.

caseStudies.headline: Discovery into the insurance placing platform
caseStudies.summary: Leading the service design and UX team through an agile discovery into the complex Lloyd’s placing platform, run entirely remotely.
clientParas: Lloyd’s of London is the world’s specialist insurance market. Its placing platform is where brokers and underwriters negotiate and bind risk, and it is complex by any standard.
challengeParas: The discovery had to identify pain points across many stakeholder groups and define a new end-to-end customer journey, with every workshop run remotely during 2020.
objectives: Run weekly remote stakeholder workshops to identify pain points
Define and design the new overarching end-to-end customer journey
Produce personas and a detailed journey map
Manage complex stakeholder relationships and the wider team during discovery
approachParas: We led the service design and UX team through an agile discovery, running stakeholder workshops weekly over Zoom and Teams. We researched key stakeholders, mapped the detailed journey in Miro and presented the final output, including personas, while managing the stakeholder relationships and the wider team.
resultParas: Lloyd’s had a defined end-to-end journey, personas and a prioritised set of pain points to take into design. Engagement ran from June to September 2020.

caseStudies.headline: To-be customer journeys for the Market Hub service
caseStudies.summary: Persona research, usability studies on wireframe prototypes and to-be journey mapping for Shell’s lubricants division.
clientParas: Shell’s fuel lubricants division was developing Market Hub, a new digital service for its business customers, with the Foolproof agency.
challengeParas: The team needed to understand its customer personas, test the wireframe prototypes of the new designs and define the to-be customer journey before build.
objectives: Research customer personas
Run usability studies on the wireframe prototypes
Map the to-be customer journey
approachParas: We completed persona research, ran usability studies to test the wireframe prototypes of the new designs and mapped the to-be customer journey in Miro, working as part of the agency team.
resultParas: The Market Hub team had validated prototypes and a to-be journey to build against. Engagement ran from November 2020 to March 2021.

caseStudies.headline: Usability testing the pre-pay proposition
caseStudies.summary: End-to-end usability testing of the Lebara mobile pre-pay proposition with sixteen participants, for the Foolproof agency.
clientParas: Lebara Mobile serves customers who need affordable pre-pay mobile and international calling.
challengeParas: The pre-pay proposition needed a fast, rigorous usability study and a report the client could act on immediately.
objectives: Plan and run end-to-end usability tests with sixteen participants
Produce a final output report for presentation to the client
approachParas: We ran the end-to-end usability tests for sixteen participants and produced the final report, which was presented to the client.
resultParas: Lebara had a prioritised list of usability findings for the proposition. Engagement completed in March 2021.

caseStudies.headline: Building and launching an AI storyboarding product
caseStudies.summary: Our own AI product: an automated storyboarding tool, taken from idea to a beta launch under the MyStoryboarder name.
clientParas: MyStoryboarder is a product we built ourselves: an AI-based tool that turns a script or brief into a storyboard automatically, for film, advertising and UX teams who need to visualise ideas quickly.
challengeParas: Generative image models made automated storyboarding possible, but a useful product needed consistent characters and scenes, an interface that non-designers could use and a sustainable cost per storyboard.
objectives: Prove that current AI models could produce usable, consistent storyboards
Design a workflow that a writer or producer could use without design skills
Launch a beta to real users and learn from their behaviour
Explore a further proof-of-concept AI tool alongside it
approachParas: We built the product in three phases between 2023 and 2025, prototyping with current image and language models, testing with early users and iterating the workflow. The beta was backed by Amazon and launched to market as MyStoryboarder.com. The experience now informs every AI proof of concept we build for clients.
resultParas: MyStoryboarder launched to market in beta and continues to develop. It is the basis of our [rapid AI proof of concept](/services/ai/rapid-ai-proof-of-concept/) service.

caseStudies.headline: 47% uplift from optimised customer application journeys
caseStudies.summary: The Post Office wanted to provide an improved user experience for their website customers.
clientParas: The Post Office wanted to provide an improved user experience for their website customers.
We continue to help them deliver intuitive customer journeys and interfaces for their customers, improving the overall brand experience.
challengeParas: The Post Office employ our user experience, product development, testing and evaluation expertise to validate new and existing developments for their website and mobile platforms.
The main objectives of the project were to:
objectives: Determine the overall ease of use, effectiveness and proposition of the Post Office website and focus on where improvements can be made
Obtain an understanding of users’ expectations and opinions of the site through lab based user testing
Identify how effectively the site navigation supported users in the main tasks to be completed
Determine a list of actionable insight for on-going work
approachParas: We continue to undertake a rolling programme of UX testing and evaluation projects. This includes prototyping and user testing new propositions and providing recommendations on how to implement an improved customer experience of existing.

We are central to any new digital product development that the Post Office undertakes and help ensure that the customer is at the core of their proposition, improving conversion rates and customer interactions with their website.
caseStudies.quote: Working with Channel Dynamics has allowed us to gain a real insight into users’ requirements and ensure that all future digital developments put the user experience at the forefront of the proposition. They are old pros and a pleasure to work with.
caseStudies.quoteWho: Senior Manager Digital at Post Office
resultParas: As a direct result of our work, the Post Office has become more user-centric in its approach to site developments. Having watched the user testing live and seeing, first-hand, a number of unexpected site issues, they continue to implement our recommendations with great success.

caseStudies.headline: 38% improvement in website bookings
caseStudies.summary: CIPFA (Chartered Institute of Public Finance & Accountancy) is the trade body for accountants working in public sector organisations. Their 14,000 members work in 3000 companies in diverse sectors such as Education, Healthcare, Defence, Transport and Local Government in over 100 countries.
clientParas: CIPFA (Chartered Institute of Public Finance & Accountancy) is the trade body for accountants working in public sector organisations. Their 14,000 members work in 3000 companies in diverse sectors such as Education, Healthcare, Defence, Transport and Local Government in over 100 countries.
challengeParas: CIPFA were interested in working with Channel Dynamics to help move the User Experience of their digital proposition forward to make it more customer centred and ensure that any new designs would be responsive and work on mobile, tablet and web.

They believed that user journeys are not as logical as they could be and that some of the content contained within these sections could be better represented or were missing. CIPFA also wanted to re-design the navigation and Information Architecture (IA) as part of the project to make it simpler for users to find relevant content.
approachParas: Channel Dynamics approached the project in a series of four agile sprints, consisting of auditing the existing content, contextual research with users and stakeholder workshops, where we identified users attitudes, motivations, behaviours and goals around the project. We analysed their existing Information Architecture (IA) and created revised site maps and navigation design which was validated with users.

Channel Dynamics also worked with the CIPFA team to model the ideal customer journeys based on user stories and customer research and created revised landing page templates, wireframes and an interactive prototype that was further tested with users in our labs. We then completed the final page designs based on user feedback and created the digital assets that could be deployed by the content team in their Content Management System (CMS).
caseStudies.quote: We asked Channel Dynamics to work with us to re-design some of the main sections of our website. The process was both logical and stimulating and helped us to get the key stakeholders on board in a series of workshops.  The site is now working on all digital devices as a result of their customer focused responsive re-designs and we highly recommend the exercise to other companies wanting to go through a similar level of change.
resultParas: As a direct result of our work, CIPFA have moved their offering forward to be much more focused around their customer needs. Users are able to find key content more easily and the internal stakeholders and members have seen a 38% uplift in conversion journeys and reduction in web queries. The client is very satisfied with the results so far and Channel Dynamics will redesign the remaining elements of the site later this year.

caseStudies.headline: 19% improvement in the number of donations
caseStudies.summary: The Royal British Legion (RBL) approached us to help them optimize the donations journey across their mobile, web and tablet devices. We developed a prototype with some suggested changes to test with users before implementation, followed by A/B testing work to further refine the process.
clientParas: The Royal British Legion (RBL) approached us to help them optimize the donations journey across their mobile, web and tablet devices. We developed a prototype with some suggested changes to test with users before implementation, followed by A/B testing work to further refine the process.
challengeParas: The Royal British Legion wanted to work with our experienced UX consultants to optimise the donations journey for their key persona groups.
The main objectives were to:
objectives: Identify a list of UX improvements for the existing donations journey
Focus the donations journey around the needs of their core persona groups
Develop these changes into a revised interactive prototype to test with users
Identify any potential issues through usability testing and modify the prototype to take these changes into consideration ready for implementation
Optimise the user journey using A/B testing to increase the number of donations
approachParas: We started the process with an end to end review of the existing donations journey based on the requirements of their user personas following a number of 1:1 interviews.
We also performed an expert review of the process to identify any potential missed opportunities for improving the overall conversion rate to donation.

We consolidated this information and built it into an interactive clickable prototype that was then used as the basis of discussion during usability testing. These sessions informed us of the effectiveness of the potential changes and identified additional areas for improvement that had not been identified. The prototype was updated and the developers used this to inform the final website changes.

Following the implementation of the journey modifications we worked with the client team to make some additional improvements through A/B testing. Our preferred tool of choice for this is Optimizely, although we can also use Visual Web Optimizer.
caseStudies.quote: Channel Dynamics were able to guide us through the optimisation of the Legion donations journey. They were professional in their approach and identified new areas of focus for our activities. We will definitely work with them again for future phases of the website development.
caseStudies.quoteWho: Digital Manager at Royal British Legion
resultParas: The changes led to a 19% improvement in the number of donations made through the website, and this is now being further optimised to better the existing control journey. This was a successful outcome for the client and provided them with a clear return on investment.

caseStudies.headline: 53% improvement for a new foreign exchange purchase journey
caseStudies.statLabel: improvement in the foreign exchange purchase journey
caseStudies.summary: First Rate, the UK’s largest provider of foreign exchange services and for many high street brands needed to improve and streamline their booking process.
clientParas: First Rate, the UK’s largest provider of foreign exchange services and for many high street brands needed to improve and streamline their booking process.
We delivered a radically simplified process moving from 8 stages and six pages, to a single transactional page.
challengeParas: First Rate (part of the Bank of Ireland) needed to optimize their web and mobile offerings. They were losing transactions and revenue due to their extended purchase process. Customers were dropping out and shopping for the cheapest foreign currency.
The main objectives of the project were to:
objectives: Improve the current order process funnel to increase the overall conversion rate to sale and reduce the current drop off rate
Integrate the same day currency order and collection concept into the existing buying process
Develop the template for white label users, with and without the same day currency collection option
Develop a proposition that can be used across platforms on both mobile and tablet
approachParas: We ran a number of ideation workshops and delivered interactive prototypes based on UX best practice, testing the proposition with their target user base. This provided real insight into customer behaviours and needs and shaped the final proposition for implementation of a streamlined purchase process.
caseStudies.quote: The process of working with Channel Dynamics has been an invaluable experience. We moved from idea to user tested interactive prototypes in a couple of weeks. The IT team were able to build the final proposition with the confidence that it would be right for users.
caseStudies.quoteWho: Head of Marketing and Retail Channels at First Rate
resultParas: Our recommendations and proposals for a revised booking process meant that the same proposition could be implemented across all digital platforms. This is having a radical impact on the method and speed that users are able to transact leading to a 53% improvement in conversion journey..

caseStudies.headline: 33% increase in membership sign-ups
caseStudies.summary: The Medical Defence Union is a medical indemnity insurance provider for their doctor members. They wanted to identify a list of quick win opportunities to increase the engagement and conversion of their website in advance of a wider design refresh. We helped them deliver improvements across their site without the need for a full website redesign.
clientParas: The Medical Defence Union is a medical indemnity insurance provider for their doctor members. They wanted to identify a list of quick win opportunities to increase the engagement and conversion of their website in advance of a wider design refresh. We helped them deliver improvements across their site without the need for a full website redesign.
challengeParas: Medical Defence Union wanted to identify a list of quick wins that could be quickly implemented on to their website.
The main objectives of the project were to:
objectives: Identify the main customer journeys and persona types that needed to be the points of focus
Undertake an heuristic analysis /expert review of the website user journeys to identify user experience problem areas
Transfer these elements into a list of actionable insight that could be implemented by the core team
Aid the implementation with a team presentation and additional consultancy days
approachParas: We had two Channel Dynamics UX consultants examine the MDU site on a detailed basis over three days. We find that it is always best to have 2-3 internal consultants examine a website to identify the maximum number of potential issues. They then underwent a peer review to agree on the priority of the issues to make sure the maximum benefit is received by the client.
We examined a range of elements from signposting, calls to action, information architecture to general design to ensure that the site was fully audited.
Channel Dynamics then turned this is to an actionable insight report and aided the implementation of the quick win list through some additional UX consultancy days.
caseStudies.quote: Channel Dynamics worked with us to deliver some quick-win improvements to the MDU website. We found that the changes were easy to implement and they had taken our technical limitations into consideration when developing the actions. Their follow up support was also very useful as they were always on hand to answer any questions we had.
caseStudies.quoteWho: Head of Digital at the Medical Defence Union
resultParas: The Medical Defence Union saw an immediate benefit as a result of the website changes with improved customer engagement, website dwell time and a 33% improvement in the membership sign up area. The MDU we pleased that their main objectives for the work had been delivered.

caseStudies.headline: 14% improvement in new player sign-ups
caseStudies.summary: BetVictor contacted Channel Dynamics to help them to understand the attitudes, motivations and behaviours of their key user personas groups for each of their Betting propositions. These were used to develop the UK and international service offerings. We then worked to re-design the key landing page triggers and increase conversion rates for new user subscriptions
clientParas: BetVictor contacted Channel Dynamics to help them to understand the attitudes, motivations and behaviours of their key user personas groups for each of their Betting propositions. These were used to develop the UK and international service offerings. We then worked to re-design the key landing page triggers and increase conversion rates for new user subscriptions
challengeParas: BetVictor is a sports book betting provider based in Gibraltar with a UK and Asian based user base. They were interested in utilising our experience of persona development and commercially focused UX design to help focus their future product development.
The main objectives were to:
objectives: Identify the attitudes, motivations and behaviours of their three focus areas of Football, Horse Racing and Casino personas
Undertake a series of deep dive interviews with these core users to establish patterns
Summarise the information and identify user journey conversion triggers that could be integrated into future product designs
Develop those learnings into modified user journeys and improved on-page conversion rates
approachParas: We ran a workshop with the BetVictor team in Gibraltar to identify the initial project focus and to identify what they already knew about their users. This is allowed us to uncover all the stakeholder insight and is an invaluable part of providing focus for the persona research sessions and the associated discussion guide.

We ran a series of individual video interviews in our research labs that explored a range of areas from why people bet through to a typical day in the life of the various users to identify key user journey information.

We translated the BetVictor insight into tangible information that could be utilised to influence the customer conversion decisions throughout the sign-up processes. We further optimised the conversion journey through A/B testing.
caseStudies.quote: Our recent projects with Channel Dynamics have gone very well. We now have a new user focus for future product developments and understand the sports book users in more detail. They helped us translate the research into clear revenue benefits and look forward to working with them again shortly.
resultParas: The new detailed personas provided actionable insight into how the conversion journeys could be modified, leading to a 14% improvement in new player sign ups and tangible efficiency and revenue benefits.

caseStudies.headline: 82% approval rating from new recruits
caseStudies.summary: The Metropolitan Police approached us to help them to help design and validate a new responsive website service for new potential recruits. They wanted to design and validate the proposition and key user journeys before launch.
clientParas: The Metropolitan Police approached us to help them to help design and validate a new responsive website service for new potential recruits. They wanted to design and validate the proposition and key user journeys before launch.
challengeParas: The Metropolitan Police wanted to use our experience of user research to inform them of the most appropriate next steps.
The main objectives of the project were to:
objectives: Validate the proposition with some of the sectors that are more difficult to recruit from such as females and people from diverse ethnic backgrounds
Identify the main user journeys and functionality required to complete the recruitment process
Identify any information gaps such as inappropriate terminology or imagery through moderated usability testing
Provide an action list of next steps to implement before the final service iteration went live
approachParas: We initially identified the elements of the proposition that the Police team wanted to validate through a short workshop with the client. Understanding the key tasks users will need to complete enabled us to start to understand the type of functional requirements that would aid successful completion of the user journeys.

We were then able to use the output information to begin constructing a discussion guide for the moderated usability research. This was then used as a framework for the research sessions. We also referenced the Metropolitan Police persona groups to add further context to the elements to be reviewed. We were able to deliver on a challenging recruitment brief to find users in 15 different representative ethnically diverse user groupings.

The user research sessions were run by Channel Dynamics moderators in our in-house testing facilities over a three day period. During the interviews, users were encouraged to discuss their actions to give a better idea of their motivations and thought process for using the new recruitment facility.
caseStudies.quote: Channel Dynamics helped us research and validate our new recruitment service platform on mobile tablet and web before we launched to make sure that the functionality and details were correct before we sent the service live. We were impressed with their professionalism and the sessions were well managed by the team and our post implementation research showed a very high approval rating with new users.

pages.name: Card sorting
pages.title: Card Sorting
intro: An Information Architecture (IA) technique, whereby your target audience labels and groups cards to help organise the structure of your site

We use card sorting to help design or investigate the information architecture of a website we’re working on. In a card sort session, participants organise cards into groups that make sense to them. We also ask them to label these groups.
We conduct card sorts with index cards, pieces of paper, Post-Its or one of several online card-sorting software tools.

sections.heading: Key benefits of running a Card Sort with Channel Dynamics
bullets: Understand your users’ expectations and understanding of your website
Customers design your information architecture in a way that makes sense to them
Use these insights to develop the structure for your website
Help refine the language and key terms you use on your website
Decide what to put on various pages and how to prioritise that information hierarchically
Helps you label sections, categories and navigation
This builds findability, efficiency and effectiveness into your site architecture

sections.heading: Open and Closed Card Sorts
paras: In an open card sort, participants create their own headings for the grouped cards. This helps you understand how your audience classifies the cards, but also what terms they use to describe the categories. This is useful for your navigation structure.

In contrast, in a closed card sort, participants are provided with a pre-defined set of category names. They then assign the index cards to these fixed categories. This helps reveal the degree to which the participants agree on which cards belong under each category.
Sometimes it’s useful to conduct an open card sort first (to identify content categories) and then use a closed card sort to see how well the category labels work.

sections.heading: Online Testing Software
paras: Many of our card sorts are carried out “live”, in-person but if you have geographically distributed users, online sessions can be useful too.
We’ve tried a few online card sorting applications over the years. If you haven’t already started testing we’ll look at which solution is best for you.

intro: If you’re not testing something then you’re wasting time – Always Be Testing

sections.heading: What is A/B or Split Testing?
paras: A/B testing pits one design against another and uses statistical analysis to determine the winner. Testing in this manner can help resolve differences of opinion arising from personal preference. Significant conversion improvements can be achieved through testing alternative elements like copy text, layouts, images and colours, or even merging / splitting pages or removing form fields.

sections.heading: What is Multivariate Testing?
paras: Multivariate testing (MVT) tests the effectiveness of numerous combinations of different elements on a page. By looking at the results from different tests, it is possible to identify those elements that consistently produce the greatest increase in conversions. MVT works particularly well with high traffic volume e-commerce websites where product inventory can be shown in different ways.

sections.heading: Key benefits of A/B & Multivariate Testing with Channel Dynamics
bullets: Remove guesswork in design decisions
Work an existing digital product’s performance harder

sections.heading: Make the most impact: A/B & MVT as business as usual
paras: It’s sometimes suggested that A/B testing stands for “Always Be Testing. If you’re not testing something then you’re wasting time. Therefore a testing programme is most effective when run as a business as usual (BAU) programme with monthly and quarterly reporting.
A typical project within a BAU programme lasts between from 5-15 working days from kick-off to report. Some tests can be launched the same day. Learning builds on learning and increases performance.

intro: Improve your digital products (websites, mobile apps & software) for your target users. We start with your objectives, pens & paper and move to prototypes tested on real people

sections.heading: Benefits of Good User Interface (UI) Design
paras: At Channel Dynamics we believe in simplification combined with consistency to make intuitive user interfaces that perform key tasks well. bullets: Your new designs will actively increase sales

sections.heading: Our Four Stage Agile UI Design Process
paras: When designing user interfaces, we generally follow a four stage agile based User Interface (UI) Design process that moves the design from the initial concept stages through to final designs.

We start with Contextual Research, where we find out as much background information as we can about your users, products and stakeholders. We identify attitudes, motivations, behaviour and goals of the users and are able to validate their user persona groupings. This gives us a solid view on the current situation and we are able to move forward from this solid foundation.

The next stage of the process involves starting with paper to sketch up some ideas. The reason we do this is because it’s cheap, quick and easy to change.  We make sure the overall foundations and interactions of the user interface is correct first and like to test with users as often as possible to enable us to work in fast iterations.

As we move through the process, we increase the fidelity of the user interface and add the final visual design on to the proposition at the end. Although it is important to have nice designs, it is essential to get the other elements correct first.

pages.name: Wireframing
pages.title: Wireframing
intro: Creating wireframes is a key element for most UX design projects. A wireframe is a representation of what users will see on the screen. Wireframes are the ultimate UX artefact, they don’t take much time to create and you can share them with your team and discuss elements on the early stages of design.

Wireframes are very powerful, you can quickly create a prototype and test interactions, labels, layouts or any other elements of your interface. This can help us identify usability issues before building the product, which is far more cost and time-effective than other traditional design methods. Normally wireframes don’t have any colour, and use a standard typeface, these visual design details will come later on the design process. Once you have agreed with your team the layout, hierarchy, content and interactions, you can move on and increase the fidelity of your wireframes.

pages.title: AI readiness health check and action plan
intro: Before anyone buys a licence or hires a data scientist, find out whether your organisation is actually ready for AI. In two to three weeks we assess your services, data, people and risk, and give you a prioritised 90-day action plan.
It is the same idea as our analytics health check: a fixed-fee, independent look at what you have, what is broken and what would make the most difference first.

sections.heading: What we look at
bullets: **Services and journeys.** Where your users wait, repeat themselves or give up, and whether AI could remove that friction or simply move it.
**Data.** Whether the data an AI feature would need exists, is accurate, is permitted for that use and is accessible to the team that would build it.
**People and skills.** Who in the organisation would own an AI service, what they can do today and what support they need.
**Risk and governance.** Data protection, bias, transparency obligations and, for public bodies, how the work would stand up at a Service Standard assessment.
**Technology.** What you already pay for that has AI capability you are not using, and where a small proof of concept beats a platform purchase.

sections.heading: What you get
paras: A short written report with a traffic-light readiness score across the five areas, the three to five opportunities most likely to pay back, the risks to resolve first, and a 90-day action plan with owners and effort estimates. We present it to your leadership team and stay available to help you act on it.

sections.heading: Who it is for

pages.name: AI opportunity discovery
pages.title: AI opportunity discovery
intro: Most AI projects fail because they start from the technology rather than the user. We start from the journey. By mapping how people and staff actually move through a service, we find the moments where an assistant, automation or decision support would help, and the moments where a human must stay in the loop.
The output is a service blueprint with AI touchpoints designed in, each with a clear user need, a data source, a fallback and an owner.

sections.heading: How it works
paras: **Discover.** Interviews, observation and analytics to map the as-is journey for users and for the staff behind the scenes.
**Locate.** Workshops with your team to identify the pain points where AI could realistically help, scored by user value, feasibility and risk.
**Design.** A to-be journey and blueprint showing where AI sits, how it hands over to people, what happens when it is wrong and how you would measure it.
**Decide.** A prioritised backlog of opportunities, each sized as a proof of concept, so you can test the strongest one next.

sections.heading: Typical opportunities we find
bullets: Triage and routing of enquiries so people reach the right team first time
Drafting and summarising for case workers, with human review
Guided eligibility checks and form completion
Search and retrieval across policy, guidance and product content
Proactive notifications based on a user’s stage in a journey
Back-office classification that frees staff time for the complex cases

sections.heading: What you get
paras: A blueprint of the service with AI touchpoints, a scored opportunity backlog, and a recommendation for the first proof of concept. Everything is written so that product, policy and technology teams can act on it without us in the room.

pages.name: Rapid AI proof of concept
pages.title: Rapid AI proof of concept
intro: The fastest way to know whether an AI idea is worth building is to put a working version in front of real users. We build proof-of-concept prototypes with current AI models in days, test them with your users and give you a decision you can defend.

This is how we built Compass for the Department of Health and Social Care, helping NHS clinicians and procurement teams choose medical devices from trusted evidence, and how we launched MyStoryboarder, an AI storyboarding product, to market in beta.

sections.heading: What a proof of concept includes
bullets: A working prototype built on current large language models or image models, connected to sample data where that is safe to do
Prompt, flow and interface design so the prototype feels like a real service, not a demo
Moderated usability sessions with representative users, including people with accessibility needs
An honest evaluation: usefulness, accuracy, failure modes, cost per interaction and what it would take to build properly
A recommendation to proceed, pivot or stop, with the evidence to show your stakeholders

sections.heading: Why a prototype before a platform
paras: A proof of concept costs a fraction of a procurement and answers the question that matters: do users trust it and does it change the outcome? It also exposes data gaps and governance questions early, when they are cheap to fix. For public sector teams it gives an alpha phase something concrete to assess.

sections.heading: How quickly
paras: A first version in one to two weeks. Testing and evaluation in the following two. Most proof-of-concept engagements are complete within six weeks.

pages.name: Conversational & agent design
pages.title: Conversational and agent experience design
intro: Chat assistants and agents are services, and they fail for the same reasons other services fail: unclear purpose, poor handling of errors and no way to reach a human. We design the conversation, the hand-offs and the trust signals, then test them with real users.
Our background in content design, usability testing and service blueprinting is exactly what conversational products need and usually lack.

sections.heading: What we design
bullets: **Purpose and scope.** What the assistant is for, what it will refuse and how it introduces itself.
**Conversation flows.** Prompts, questions, confirmations and summaries written in plain language and tested with users.
**Error and uncertainty handling.** What happens when the model is unsure, wrong or out of scope, and how a person takes over.
**Trust signals.** Sources, confidence, transparency about AI use and clear routes to a human.
**Measurement.** Task completion, containment, satisfaction and quality review, so you know whether it is working after launch.

sections.heading: Evaluation
paras: We run moderated sessions where users complete real tasks with the assistant, and we review transcripts against a quality rubric covering accuracy, tone, safety and recovery. The findings feed directly into the prompts, flows and interface.

We are candid about the limits. Synthetic users are not users, and a model summarising ten interviews is not the same as a researcher who sat in them.

sections.heading: Where it does not
bullets: Replacing participants with synthetic personas
Deciding what the findings mean without a researcher checking the source

pages.name: Responsible AI for services

**Fairness.** Testing outcomes across user groups, including people with accessibility needs and those in vulnerable circumstances.
**Transparency.** Plain-language explanations for users, records for the transparency register and meaningful ways to challenge a decision.
**Operations.** Monitoring, quality review and escalation once the service is live.
